title: Building a Lao Language LLM with Gemma 4: A Complete Guide
excerpt: How I fine-tuned Google's Gemma 4 E4B model to understand and generate Lao text — covering vocab surgery, continual pre-training, and supervised fine-tuning from scratch.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Lao is a language that the AI world has largely forgotten. With fewer than 100 million speakers and a shortage of digitized text, building a language model from scratch just didn't make sense — too expensive, too inefficient, and frankly, not the smartest use of resources.
So I took a different approach. Instead of starting from zero, I took Google's Gemma 4 E4B — a capable 4-billion-parameter multimodal model — and essentially taught it Lao. Step by step, I adapted a model built for dominant, western-centric languages into something that could actually read, understand, and write fluent Lao.

sections.title: Step 1 — Collect Lao Language Data
sections.body:
Step 1 is the full data-engineering pipeline that turns noisy web text into a tokenizer-ready Lao corpus.

Step 1.1) Define source strategy and output contract.
Goal: collect broad Lao language coverage (encyclopedic + news + domain text) and produce deterministic raw artifacts.
```python
SOURCES = {
    "wikipedia": "lo.wikipedia.org",
    "news": ["kpl.gov.la", "vientianemai.com"],
    "domain": ["banking_docs", "public_notices"],
    "eval": ["FLORES-200"],
}
RAW_DIR = "data/raw"
PROCESSED_DIR = "data/processed"
```

Step 1.2) Collect raw Lao text from each source with traceability.
```python
from subprocess import run

run(["python", "tools/data_collection/collect_wikipedia.py", "--output", "data/raw/wiki_lao.txt"], check=True)
run(["python", "tools/data_collection/collect_news.py", "--group", "newspapers", "--max-pages", "50"], check=True)
run(["python", "tools/data_collection/collect_news.py", "--source", "kpl", "--cat", "1", "--max-pages", "30"], check=True)
```

Step 1.3) Normalize each fetched file independently (Unicode, Lao-ratio filtering, dedup).
```python
from pathlib import Path
from subprocess import run

for src in Path("data/raw").glob("*.txt"):
    dst = Path("data/processed") / f"{src.stem}_clean.txt"
    run([
        "python", "scripts/normalize_lao.py",
        str(src), str(dst), "--filter-lao", "0.30", "--dedup"
    ], check=True)
```

Step 1.4) Run quality checks before merge (minimum length, Lao ratio, duplicate drift).
```python
from pathlib import Path

stats = {}
for p in Path("data/processed").glob("*_clean.txt"):
    lines = [x.strip() for x in p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() if x.strip()]
    stats[p.name] = {"lines": len(lines), "sample": lines[0][:120] if lines else ""}
print(stats)
```

Step 1.5) Merge cleaned shards into one training corpus.
```python
from pathlib import Path

parts = [p.read_text(encoding="utf-8") for p in Path("data/processed").glob("*_clean.txt")]
Path("data/processed/all_lao_clean.txt").write_text("\n".join(parts), encoding="utf-8")
```

Step 1.6) Train tokenizer from merged corpus.
```python
from subprocess import run

run([
    "python", "models/tokenizer/train_tokenizer.py",
    "--corpus", "data/processed/all_lao_clean.txt",
    "--output-dir", "models/tokenizer/lao_tokenizer_v1"
], check=True)
```

Step 1.7) Validate tokenizer behavior before model surgery.
```python
from subprocess import run

run([
    "python", "models/tokenizer/train_tokenizer.py",
    "--test-only",
    "--model-dir", "models/tokenizer/lao_tokenizer_v1/hf_tokenizer"
], check=True)
```

Example output (short):
```bash
Raw files: 12
Processed files: 12
Merged corpus: data/processed/all_lao_clean.txt
Tokenizer vocab: 32,000
Tokenizer test: PASS
```

Result: a reproducible, audited, tokenizer-ready Lao corpus and a validated tokenizer model for downstream vocab surgery/CPT.

Credit: data collection inspiration and source references from GitHub user therngbtg (https://github.com/therngbtg), LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/in/bountherng-phetlasy-489a3316b/).

sections.title: Step 2 — Tokenizer Audit and Vocab Surgery
sections.body:
Step 2 is the full tokenizer surgery workflow after Step 1 data collection and normalization. First, I extract Lao tokens that exist in my tokenizer but do not exist in Gemma 4. Then I clean noisy tokens, add clean Lao tokens to Gemma, validate before/after tokenization quality, and save a new surgery-ready base model.

Step 2.1) Extract missing Lao tokens from Gemma.
```python
import json
import sentencepiece as spm
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

gemma_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google/gemma-4-E4B", trust_remote_code=True)
lao_sp = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file="lao_spm.model")

def is_lao(text):
    return any("\u0e80" <= ch <= "\u0eff" for ch in text)

lao_vocab = [lao_sp.id_to_piece(i) for i in range(lao_sp.get_piece_size())]
lao_vocab = [t for t in lao_vocab if is_lao(t)]
new_tokens = sorted([t for t in lao_vocab if t not in gemma_tok.get_vocab()])

json.dump({"tokens": new_tokens, "gemma_original_vocab": len(gemma_tok)}, open("lao_missing_tokens.json", "w", encoding="utf-8"), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
```

Step 2.2) Clean missing tokens (remove noisy tokens before surgery).
```python
import json

data = json.load(open("lao_missing_tokens.json", "r", encoding="utf-8"))
raw_tokens = data["tokens"]

def is_clean_lao_token(token):
    t = token.replace("▁", "")
    if not t or len(t) > 30:
        return False
    if t[0] in '()[]{}.,;:!?"\'/\\@#$%^&*+=<>~`' or t[-1] in '()[]{}.,;:!?"\'/\\@#$%^&*+=<>~`':
        return False
    if any(c in t for c in "()[]{}"):
        return False
    lao_chars = sum(1 for c in t if 0x0E80 <= ord(c) <= 0x0EFF)
    return lao_chars > 0 and lao_chars / len(t) >= 0.5

clean_tokens = sorted([t for t in raw_tokens if is_clean_lao_token(t)])
json.dump({"tokens": clean_tokens, "gemma_original_vocab": data["gemma_original_vocab"], "new_vocab_size": data["gemma_original_vocab"] + len(clean_tokens)}, open("lao_missing_tokens_clean.json", "w", encoding="utf-8"), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
```

Step 2.3) Load clean missing tokens and add them to Gemma tokenizer.
```python
import json
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

MODEL_ID = "google/gemma-4-E4B"
token_data = json.load(open("lao_missing_tokens_clean.json", "r", encoding="utf-8"))
new_tokens = token_data["tokens"]

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID, trust_remote_code=True)
original_vocab_size = len(tokenizer)
num_added = tokenizer.add_tokens(new_tokens)
print(f"Vocab size: {original_vocab_size} -> {len(tokenizer)} (+{num_added})")
```

Step 2.4) Before vs after surgery comparison.
```python
original_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)

test_texts = [
    "ສະບາຍດີ",
    "ນະຄອນຫຼວງວຽງຈັນ ເປັນນະຄອນຫລວງຂອງປະເທດລາວ",
    "ພາສາລາວມີ 27 ພະຍັນຊະນະ",
    "How can I help you today?",
]
for text in test_texts:
    old_tokens = original_tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    new_tokens_after = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    reduction = ((len(old_tokens) - len(new_tokens_after)) / len(old_tokens)) * 100
    print(text, f"-> {len(old_tokens)} to {len(new_tokens_after)} ({reduction:.1f}% reduction)")
```

Step 2.5) Save surgery model for next CPT step.
```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
import os

OUTPUT_DIR = "./models/gemma4_lao_base_v1"
os.makedirs(OUTPUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID, trust_remote_code=True)
model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer))
model.save_pretrained(OUTPUT_DIR, max_shard_size="2GB", safe_serialization=True)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(OUTPUT_DIR)
```

Example output:
```bash
Missing Lao tokens to add: 28,022
Gemma original vocab:      262,144
New vocab size:            290,166

BEFORE vs AFTER SURGERY
- ສະບາຍດີ: 4 -> 2 tokens (50.0% reduction)
- ນະຄອນຫຼວງວຽງຈັນ...: 24 -> 4 tokens (83.3% reduction)
- ພາສາລາວມີ 27...: 15 -> 6 tokens (60.0% reduction)
- How can I help you today?: 7 -> 7 tokens (0.0% reduction)

SURGERY SUMMARY
Vocab size: 262,144 -> 290,166 (+28,022)
Saved to: ./models/gemma4_lao_base_v1
```

Actual results from my run: missing Lao tokens = 31,279, cleaned tokens added = 28,022, and Gemma vocab changed from 262,144 to 290,166. Tokenization improved significantly on Lao sentences, while English tokenization stayed unchanged.

sections.title: Step 3 — Continual Pre-Training (CPT)
sections.body:
Step 3 is Continual Pre-Training (CPT) on Lao corpus using the surgery base model from Step 2. In simple terms: Step 2 fixes tokenization, and Step 3 teaches those new Lao tokens with real Lao context so the model can predict Lao text naturally.

Step 3.1) Check GPU and load the surgery base model in 4-bit mode.
```python
import torch
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel

print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else "No GPU")
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name="AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-base-v1",
    max_seq_length=512,
    dtype=torch.float16,
    load_in_4bit=True,
    token=True,
    fix_tokenizer=False,
)
```

Step 3.2) Add QLoRA adapters and train on normalized Lao corpus.
```python
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import TrainingArguments, DataCollatorForLanguageModeling
from trl import SFTTrainer

model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0, bias="none", use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth", random_state=42,
    target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj","gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj","embed_tokens","lm_head"])

dataset = load_dataset("text", data_files="lao_merged_corpus_normalized.txt", split="train")
dataset = dataset.filter(lambda x: len(x["text"].strip()) > 10)

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    train_dataset=dataset.map(lambda e: {"input_ids": tokenizer(e["text"], truncation=True, max_length=512)["input_ids"], "labels": tokenizer(e["text"], truncation=True, max_length=512)["input_ids"]}),
    dataset_text_field=None,
    data_collator=DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(tokenizer=tokenizer, mlm=False),
    args=TrainingArguments(output_dir="./checkpoints/lao_cpt", num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=1, gradient_accumulation_steps=16, learning_rate=2e-4, fp16=True, optim="adamw_8bit", report_to="none"),
    max_seq_length=512,
)
trainer.train()
```

Step 3.3) Save LoRA + merged checkpoints, then run quick sanity generation.
```python
save_path = "./models/gemma4_lao_cpt_v1"
model.save_pretrained(save_path + "_lora")
model.save_pretrained_merged(save_path + "_merged", tokenizer, save_method="merged_16bit")

FastLanguageModel.for_inference(model)
```

Example output (short):
```bash
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090
Total samples after filter: 53,000
Training: 3 epochs | final loss ~0.60
Saved: ./models/gemma4_lao_cpt_v1_lora
Saved: ./models/gemma4_lao_cpt_v1_merged
```

Result: after CPT, the model is Lao-aware at the language-modeling level and ready for Step 4 supervised fine-tuning.

sections.title: Step 4 — Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
sections.body:
Step 4 is Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): after CPT teaches language structure, SFT teaches assistant behavior (instruction-following, clearer answers, chat alignment).

Pipeline status in my project:
```bash
Step 1: Vocab Surgery -> AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-base-v1
Step 2: CPT          -> AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-cpt-v1
Step 3: SFT          -> AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-instruct-v1
```

Step 4.1) Use CPT output as base and train SFT LoRA on Lao instruction data.
```python
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel

model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name="AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-base-v1",
    max_seq_length=512,
    load_in_4bit=True,
    token=True,
)
# then load CPT adapter, merge, and run SFT training on alpaca_lao_sft_3000.jsonl
```

Step 4.2) Save and upload SFT adapter.
```python
# Output adapter repo
# AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-instruct-v1
```

Step 4.3) Inference with Gemma chat format.
```python
def ask(question):
    text = f"<start_of_turn>user\n{question}<end_of_turn>\n<start_of_turn>model\n"
    # tokenize + generate
```

Example output (short):
```bash
Dataset: 2,999 samples
Epochs: 3 | Steps: 564
Loss: 0.4978 -> 0.4275 (-16.9%)
Training time: ~49 min on RTX 4090
Cost: ~$0.24
Saved adapter: AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-instruct-v1
```

Result: `gemma-4-lao-instruct-v1` becomes instruction-following and ready to merge into a single full model.

sections.title: Step 5 — Merge and Evaluate
sections.body:
Step 5 is Merge and Evaluate: merge CPT + SFT adapters into one standalone model so deployment is simpler (single repo, no adapter stacking at runtime).

Step 5.1) Load base model in full precision (no 4-bit) for safe merge.
```python
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name="AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-base-v1",
    max_seq_length=512,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    load_in_4bit=False,
    token=True,
)
```

Step 5.2) Apply and merge CPT adapter, then SFT adapter.
```python
# Merge CPT -> merge_and_unload()
# Merge SFT -> merge_and_unload()
```

Step 5.3) Quick QA sanity test (Lao + English prompts), then save merged model.
```python
model.save_pretrained_merged("./gemma4-lao-full", tokenizer, save_method="merged_16bit")
```

Step 5.4) Upload full model.
```python
# Repo: AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full
```

Example output (short):
```bash
CPT merged: ✅
SFT merged: ✅
Saved: ./gemma4-lao-full
Uploaded: AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full
```

Result: one full Lao Gemma model (`AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full`) that can be loaded directly with `AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(...)`.

sections.title: Lessons Learned
sections.body:
Reflecting on the full build, five engineering lessons stand out:
1. Vocabulary surgery is mandatory for Lao. Without adding missing Lao tokens, token fragmentation is severe and both context efficiency and training quality degrade quickly.
2. Clean data beats big data. A normalized and deduplicated Lao corpus (published as `AOYPSK/lao_text_corpus`) gave far better downstream behavior than noisy web text.
3. Two-stage adaptation works well for low-resource languages: CPT first for language structure, then SFT for assistant behavior.
4. Adapter-based training is cost-effective. QLoRA + staged merging made it practical to iterate quickly on consumer-grade cloud GPUs.
5. Evaluation must be bilingual and domain-specific. The model can stay strong in English while improving Lao fluency, but factual reliability still depends heavily on high-quality Lao instruction data.

sections.title: What's Next
sections.body:
The current public artifacts on Hugging Face are:
- Full model: `AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full`
- Lao corpus dataset: `AOYPSK/lao_text_corpus`

Next priorities are:
1. Expand instruction data with native human-written Lao QA and task-style prompts (reduce hallucination on local topics).
2. Run formal benchmark suites for both fluency and factuality (including Lao-specific and cross-lingual checks).
3. Build an OCR + document understanding pipeline on top of `AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full` for real Lao document workflows.
4. Export optimized inference formats (GGUF / quantized variants) for lower-cost deployment on local and edge environments.

title: The Absolute Beginner’s Guide to Flutter: From Zero to First App (iOS & Android)
excerpt: A practical beginner guide to set up Flutter on Windows and macOS, run your first app on iOS and Android, and avoid common environment setup issues.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Flutter is a game-changer for cross-platform development, especially if you come from web or backend systems. But in professional teams, "it runs on my machine" is not good enough. We need a reproducible setup that every engineer (and intern) can bootstrap with minimal friction.
This guide walks through a robust Flutter setup on both Windows and macOS, with the engineering mindset I use in real projects: clean environment boundaries, deterministic tooling, and repeatable verification steps.

Platform support summary:
- macOS: can build for both iOS and Android. Required if you want to ship to the App Store.
- Windows: can build for Android only. iOS builds require a Mac (or a remote macOS build server / CI like Codemagic / GitHub Actions macOS runners).

sections.title: Phase 1 — Environment Philosophy and Prerequisites
sections.body:
Start with a dedicated development directory to avoid permission conflicts and scattered SDK paths.

**macOS / Linux:**
```bash
mkdir -p ~/Dev
cd ~/Dev
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**
```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path C:\Dev
Set-Location C:\Dev
```
Keep the path short and free of spaces (e.g., `C:\Dev`, not `C:\Users\My Name\Documents\Dev`). Long paths and spaces are a common source of obscure Flutter / Gradle errors on Windows.

Core prerequisites (both OS):
1) Visual Studio Code (recommended editor for speed + extension ecosystem).
2) Git (required to clone Flutter SDK and manage channel upgrades cleanly).
3) Android Studio (Android SDK, AVD, command-line tools).
4) JDK 17 (bundled with recent Android Studio; otherwise install separately).

macOS only:
5) Xcode (mandatory for iOS build/signing).
6) Optional but recommended: Homebrew for easier package management.

Windows only:
5) Enable long path support and Developer Mode (Settings → System → For developers → Developer Mode = On). This prevents the classic `path too long` and symlink errors during `flutter doctor` and Gradle builds.
6) Optional: install Chocolatey or winget for easier package management.

sections.title: Phase 2 — Installing the Flutter SDK (Git-Based)
sections.body:
For professional workflows, install Flutter SDK via Git instead of manual ZIP extraction. This gives you easier channel switching (`stable`, `beta`, `master`) and predictable updates.

**macOS / Linux:**
```bash
cd ~/Dev
git clone https://github.com/flutter/flutter.git -b stable
```
Add Flutter to PATH (zsh example):
```bash
echo 'export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/Dev/flutter/bin"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc
flutter --version
```
If you use bash instead of zsh, append the same line to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.bash_profile`.

**Windows (PowerShell):**
```powershell
Set-Location C:\Dev
git clone https://github.com/flutter/flutter.git -b stable
```
Add Flutter to PATH (user-level, no admin needed):
```powershell
$flutterBin = "C:\Dev\flutter\bin"
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(
    "Path",
    [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";$flutterBin",
    "User"
)
```
Close and reopen PowerShell, then verify:
```powershell
flutter --version
```
If `flutter` is not recognized, log out and back in (or restart) so the new PATH is picked up.

VS Code setup (both OS):
1) Install the `Flutter` extension (Dart is auto-installed).
2) Restart VS Code.
3) Confirm the extension sees the SDK path (Command Palette → `Flutter: Change SDK`).

sections.title: Phase 3a — Android Toolchain Setup (Windows & macOS)
sections.body:
The Android toolchain is identical in concept on both OSes; only the install method differs.

1) Install Android Studio (download from developer.android.com, or `brew install --cask android-studio` on macOS, or `winget install Google.AndroidStudio` on Windows).
2) Launch Android Studio once and finish the initial SDK setup wizard.
3) Open Settings/Preferences → Languages & Frameworks → Android SDK.
4) In the `SDK Tools` tab, enable:
   - `Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)`
   - `Android SDK Build-Tools`
   - `Android SDK Platform-Tools`
   - `Android Emulator`
5) Accept all SDK licenses:
```bash
flutter doctor --android-licenses
```
On Windows, run the same command in PowerShell. Type `y` and Enter for each license prompt.

6) Create an Android Virtual Device (AVD): Android Studio → Device Manager → Create Device → pick a Pixel profile + a recent system image (API 34 or 35 recommended).

Windows-specific note: enable hardware acceleration. On Intel CPUs, install `Intel HAXM` via the SDK Manager. On AMD CPUs or modern Intel, enable `Windows Hypervisor Platform` (Control Panel → Programs → Turn Windows features on or off). Without this, the emulator will be painfully slow or refuse to start.

sections.title: Phase 3b — iOS Toolchain Setup (macOS Only)
sections.body:
iOS development requires macOS. If you are on Windows, skip this phase and use a Mac, a cloud Mac service (MacStadium, MacInCloud), or CI runners (Codemagic, GitHub Actions macOS) for iOS builds.

1) Install Xcode from the Mac App Store (large download, plan for 8–15 GB).
2) Open Xcode once and complete the initial component install.
3) Set the active developer directory and accept the license:
```bash
sudo xcode-select --switch /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer
sudo xcodebuild -license accept
```
4) Install the iOS Simulator runtime (Xcode → Settings → Platforms → iOS → Get).
5) Install CocoaPods for iOS plugin dependency resolution:
```bash
sudo gem install cocoapods
pod --version
```
On Apple Silicon Macs, if you hit Ruby/FFI errors, prefer installing CocoaPods via Homebrew instead:
```bash
brew install cocoapods
```
6) Launch the simulator at least once to confirm it boots:
```bash
open -a Simulator
```

sections.title: Phase 4 — The Flutter Doctor Ritual (Verification Gate)
sections.body:
Run diagnostics and treat this as your environment unit test. Same command on both OSes:
```bash
flutter doctor
```

A healthy macOS output should show:
```bash
[✓] Flutter (Channel stable)
[✓] Android toolchain - develop for Android devices
[✓] Xcode - develop for iOS and macOS
[✓] Chrome - develop for the web
[✓] Android Studio
[✓] VS Code
[✓] Connected device
```

A healthy Windows output should show:
```bash
[✓] Flutter (Channel stable, on Microsoft Windows)
[✓] Windows Version (Windows 10/11)
[✓] Android toolchain - develop for Android devices
[✓] Chrome - develop for the web
[✓] Visual Studio - develop Windows apps (optional, only if you target Windows desktop)
[✓] Android Studio
[✓] VS Code
[✓] Connected device
```
Xcode will NOT appear on Windows — that is expected.

If any item has `[!]` or `[✗]`, fix it before creating your project. For verbose diagnostics:
```bash
flutter doctor -v
```
This single habit prevents most onboarding pain.

sections.title: Phase 5 — First Project, Run Commands, and Clean Starter App
Common Setup Errors & Fixes
sections.body:
Use this as a quick diagnostic playbook when your setup breaks.

Windows — quick fixes:
1) Error: `cmdline-tools component is missing`
Action: Android Studio -> SDK Manager -> SDK Tools -> enable `Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)`, then run:
```bash
flutter doctor --android-licenses
```

2) Error: `Unable to locate Android SDK`
Action: set `ANDROID_HOME`, reopen PowerShell:
```powershell
setx ANDROID_HOME "C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Android\Sdk"
```

3) Error: long path / symlink failures
Action: enable Developer Mode, then run:
```bash
git config --global core.longpaths true
```

4) Issue: Gradle hangs forever
Action: exclude `C:\Dev` and Flutter SDK directory from antivirus real-time scanning.

macOS — quick fixes:
1) Error: `CocoaPods not installed`
Action:
```bash
brew install cocoapods
```

2) Error: `xcrun: invalid active developer path`
Action:
```bash
sudo xcode-select --switch /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer
```

3) Issue: iOS simulator does not boot
Action: Xcode -> Settings -> Platforms -> reinstall iOS runtime.

4) Error: permission denied on shell profile
Action:
```bash
ls -la ~/.zshrc
sudo chown $(whoami) ~/.zshrc
```

sections.title: Pro Tips
sections.body:
1) Hot Reload is your feedback superpower; use it constantly during UI work.
2) On older machines, prefer physical devices over emulators to reduce memory pressure. On Windows especially, USB debugging on a real Android phone is much faster than the AVD.
3) Use `flutter pub add <package>` instead of manually editing `pubspec.yaml`.
4) Install VS Code extensions: `Awesome Flutter Snippets` and `Error Lens`.
5) For production apps, start learning Flavors early (Dev/Staging/Prod) to isolate API configs and signing safely.
6) Pin your Flutter version per project with `flutter --version` output committed to the repo (or use `fvm` for multi-version teams) so every machine — Windows or Mac — builds the same binary.

sections.title: Call to Action
sections.body:
If you are blocked by a setup error, share your `flutter doctor -v` output plus OS (Windows version or macOS version) + IDE version. Most environment failures are deterministic and fixable once diagnostics are visible.
If you want, I can write a follow-up guide on integrating AI features into Flutter using either REST APIs or on-device inference (`tflite_flutter`) with production-safe architecture.

title: B(l)utter: Flutter Mobile Application Reverse Engineering Tool
excerpt: A practical technical overview of B(l)utter for analyzing Flutter Android libapp.so, including setup, usage, and output artifact breakdown.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: B(l)utter is a Flutter mobile reverse engineering tool focused on Dart AOT runtime analysis. It is designed to inspect Flutter Android binaries (specifically `libapp.so`) and generate useful artifacts for static/dynamic analysis workflows. At the moment, support is centered on Android ARM64 and recent Dart runtime versions.

sections.title: What B(l)utter Is Good For
sections.body:
In practical security and reverse engineering workflows, B(l)utter helps you:
1) Analyze Dart AOT internals from Flutter release binaries.
2) Extract assembly and object-pool related artifacts for deeper inspection.
3) Generate a Frida script template to accelerate runtime instrumentation.
4) Build a repeatable pipeline for app triage and technical research.

sections.title: Environment Setup
sections.body:
B(l)utter requires modern C++ toolchains (for example g++ >= 13 or Clang >= 16 in current upstream notes). Linux is commonly preferred for easier setup.

Debian / Ubuntu-style setup:
```bash
apt install python3-pyelftools python3-requests git cmake ninja-build \
    build-essential pkg-config libicu-dev libcapstone-dev
```

Windows setup:
1) Install Git and Python 3.
2) Install latest Visual Studio with C++ desktop + CMake tools.
3) Install required libs (`libcapstone`, `libicu4c`) via project helper script.
```powershell
python scripts\init_env_win.py
```
Then use `x64 Native Tools Command Prompt`.

macOS setup:
```bash
brew install cmake ninja pkg-config icu4c capstone
pip3 install pyelftools requests
```
(Older macOS versions may require specific LLVM versions as documented upstream.)

sections.title: Usage Workflow
sections.body:
Extract the `lib` folder from an APK first, then run B(l)utter against `arm64-v8a`:
```bash
python3 blutter.py path/to/app/lib/arm64-v8a out_dir
```
`blutter.py` auto-detects Dart version from Flutter engine metadata and selects the matching blutter executable.
If the required executable does not exist locally, it can fetch/build dependencies automatically.

sections.title: Output Artifacts
sections.body:
Typical output files you will use in analysis:
- `asm/*`: generated libapp assemblies with symbols.
- `blutter_frida.js`: Frida template for dynamic instrumentation.
- `objs.txt`: nested object dump from object pool.
- `pp.txt`: full Dart objects in the object pool.

These artifacts provide both static visibility and runtime hook-entry context.

sections.title: Project Directory Anatomy
sections.body:
- `bin`: built blutter executables per Dart version / OS / arch.
- `blutter`: core source code.
- `build`: temporary build projects (safe to delete after build).
- `dartsdk`: checked-out Dart runtime sources (safe to delete after build).
- `external`: third-party libraries (especially relevant on Windows).
- `packages`: static libraries of Dart runtime.
- `scripts`: helper scripts for fetching/building Dart-related components.

sections.title: Operational Notes and Limits
sections.body:
Current practical limits:
1) Main support target is Android `libapp.so` ARM64.
2) Works best with recent Dart runtime versions.
3) iOS and heavily obfuscated targets may need additional manual workflows.

For updates, keep the repo synced (`git pull`) and rebuild when required.

sections.title: Reference
sections.body:
Official repository and documentation:
https://github.com/worawit/blutter

If you want, I can create a follow-up post showing a safe, legal analysis checklist (scope definition, permissions, and red-team/blue-team reporting format) for Flutter reverse engineering projects.

title: Docker for Beginners: What It Is and How to Use It
excerpt: Docker lets you run apps in containers so they work the same everywhere. Here's a simple guide to get started from zero.

sections.title: What Is Docker?
sections.body:
Docker packages your app and everything it needs into one unit called a **container** — so it runs the same on your laptop, a teammate's PC, or a cloud server.

:::compare
**Without Docker**|You install Node.js 18 locally, but production runs Node.js 16. Small mismatches can break the app.
**With Docker**|Your app ships with its own runtime inside the image. Same behavior everywhere.
:::

:::analogy
Think of it like a lunchbox:
- The **lunchbox** = container
- The **food inside** = your app + dependencies
- You can move it anywhere and it stays the same
:::

sections.title: Image vs Container — What's the Difference?
sections.body:
These two words confuse most beginners. Here is the short version:

:::defs
**Image**|A read-only blueprint — like a recipe. Downloaded from registries such as Docker Hub (hub.docker.com).
**Container**|A running instance of an image — like the meal you cooked from that recipe.
:::

One image can power many containers at the same time. Docker Hub includes ready-made images for Node.js, Python, Nginx, PostgreSQL, and more.

sections.title: Installing Docker
sections.body:
**macOS / Windows**
Download Docker Desktop:
https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/

It includes the engine, CLI, and a simple GUI.

**Ubuntu Linux**
```bash
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh
sudo sh get-docker.sh
```

Verify installation:
```bash
docker run hello-world
```

:::callout tip
If you see `Hello from Docker!` in the terminal, your setup is ready.
:::

sections.title: Run Your First Container
sections.body:
Start a real web server in one command:
```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name my-nginx nginx
```

What each flag does:
- `-d` — run in the background
- `-p 8080:80` — map port 8080 on your machine to port 80 in the container
- `--name my-nginx` — readable container name
- `nginx` — image pulled from Docker Hub automatically

Open `http://localhost:8080` — you should see the Nginx welcome page.

Handy commands:
```bash
docker ps
docker stop my-nginx
docker rm my-nginx
```

sections.title: Your First Dockerfile
sections.body:
A **Dockerfile** tells Docker how to build your own image. Minimal Node.js example:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

Build and run:
```bash
docker build -t my-app .
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 my-app
```

Your app is now running inside a container at `http://localhost:3000`.

sections.title: 3 Things to Remember as a Beginner
sections.body:
:::reminders
**Data disappears with the container**|Files stored only inside a container are lost when you delete it. Use volumes for persistence.
**Add a `.dockerignore` file**|Like `.gitignore` — exclude `node_modules`, `.env`, and `.git` from the build context.
**Clean up old images**|Containers and images accumulate quickly. Run `docker system prune -a` when you need space.
:::

Volume example:
```bash
docker run -v mydata:/app/data my-app
```

`.dockerignore` example:
```bash
node_modules
.env
.git
```

sections.title: What's Next?
sections.body:
When the basics feel comfortable, learn **Docker Compose** — one file to run multiple services together (for example API + database).

:::steps
1) Dockerize one small project you already have.
2) Try Compose with an app and PostgreSQL.
3) Read the official getting-started guide for best practices.
:::

Official docs:
https://docs.docker.com/get-started/

For me, Docker clicked when I needed the same Python ML environment on different machines — once you use it on a real repo, it makes sense fast.

title: GitHub for Beginners: Save and Share Your Code the Right Way
excerpt: GitHub is where developers save, track, and share their code. This guide walks you through the basics — from creating a repo to your first commit.

sections.title: What Is GitHub?
sections.body:
Most beginners mix these up. Here is the split:

:::defs
**Git**|Version control on your computer — tracks every change, branches, and history.
**GitHub**|Cloud hosting for Git repos — backup, sharing, pull requests, and portfolio proof.
:::

:::analogy
Think of it like Google Docs for code:
- Every save is a **commit** with a message
- You can restore any older version
- Teammates edit in parallel without overwriting each other
:::

Almost every developer role expects GitHub fluency. A public repo is often the fastest proof of what you can build.

sections.title: Installing Git
sections.body:
GitHub lives in the browser — **Git** is what you install locally.

**macOS**
```bash
brew install git
```

**Ubuntu / Debian**
```bash
sudo apt install git
```

**Windows**
https://git-scm.com/download/win

Set your identity once (used on every commit):
```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@email.com"
```

Verify:
```bash
git --version
```

:::callout tip
Match `user.email` to the email on your GitHub account so commits link to your profile.
:::

sections.title: Create Your First Repository
sections.body:
A **repository (repo)** is a project folder that Git tracks over time.

:::compare
**Start on GitHub**|Best for beginners: create the repo online, clone it, then code. You get a README and remote URL immediately.
**Start locally**|Best when you already have a folder: `git init`, then connect to GitHub later with `git remote add`.
:::

**GitHub-first workflow**
:::steps
1) Sign in at github.com → **+** → New repository
2) Name it (e.g. `my-first-repo`), pick Public or Private
3) Check **Add a README file** → Create repository
4) Clone to your machine and enter the folder
:::

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-username/my-first-repo.git
cd my-first-repo
```

**Local-first workflow**
```bash
mkdir my-project && cd my-project
git init
```

sections.title: The 3 Commands You Use Every Day
sections.body:
After editing files, ship changes in three moves — same order every time:

:::reminders
**git add .**|Stage changes (`.` = all files; or `git add index.html` for one file)
**git commit -m "message"**|Save a snapshot — message should say what changed, not just "update"
**git push**|Upload commits to GitHub so your remote repo stays current
:::

Example session:
```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add homepage layout"
git push
```

:::callout tip
Run `git status` before `add` — it shows exactly which files changed and avoids surprises.
:::

sections.title: Pulling Changes from GitHub
sections.body:
On a second laptop or with teammates, sync before you edit:
```bash
git pull
```

This downloads the latest commits from GitHub into your working copy.

:::callout tip
**Daily rhythm:** `git pull` when you start → code → `git add` / `commit` / `push` when you finish. That order prevents most merge conflicts.
:::

sections.title: Branches — Work Without Breaking Things
sections.body:
A **branch** is a safe workspace — experiment without breaking `main`.

:::compare
**main branch**|Production-ready code. What users or CI expect to be stable.
**feature branch**|In-progress work: login page, bugfix, or experiment.
:::

Create and switch:
```bash
git checkout -b my-new-feature
```

Commit and publish the branch:
```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add login page"
git push origin my-new-feature
```

On GitHub, open a **Pull Request (PR)** to merge into `main` after review.

sections.title: Useful Commands to Know
sections.body:
Keep these in muscle memory:

:::defs
**git status**|See modified, staged, and untracked files
**git log --oneline**|Compact commit history
**git diff**|Line-by-line changes before you commit
**git branch**|List local branches
**git checkout -b name**|Create and switch to a new branch
:::

Undo the last commit but keep file changes:
```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1
```

sections.title: What's Next?
sections.body:
When the basics feel natural, level up with:

:::steps
1) Add a **`.gitignore`** so secrets and `node_modules` never get committed.
2) Try **GitHub Pages** — free static hosting from any public repo.
3) Practice **Pull Requests** on a real team repo (even a friend's side project).
4) **Fork** an open-source repo, fix a small issue, and open your first PR.
:::

Official starting guide:
https://docs.github.com/en/get-started

The fastest way to learn is one real project on GitHub this week — not another tutorial.

title: Basic SQL Commands Every Developer Should Know
excerpt: SQL is the language you use to talk to databases. Learn the essential commands — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — with simple examples you can try right now.

sections.title: What Is SQL?
sections.body:
**SQL (Structured Query Language)** is how apps talk to relational databases — read, insert, update, and delete data with plain statements.

:::analogy
Think of a database like a set of spreadsheets:
- Each **table** = one sheet (users, orders, products)
- Each **row** = one record
- Each **column** = one field (name, email, age)
:::

:::defs
**PostgreSQL**|Popular in production backends and fintech
**MySQL**|Common in web apps and LAMP stacks
**SQLite**|Lightweight — mobile apps, prototypes, and learning
:::

SQL is a **query language**, not a general programming language like Python. You ask; the database answers with rows.

sections.title: Your First Table
sections.body:
Data lives in **tables** — rows and columns with a fixed schema.

Example `users` table:

```text
id | name  | email              | age
1  | Aoy   | aoy@example.com    | 24
2  | Som   | som@example.com    | 28
3  | Kham  | kham@example.com   | 22
```

Create it:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name  VARCHAR(100),
  email VARCHAR(100),
  age   INT
);
```

:::defs
**INT**|Whole numbers (age, quantity, IDs)
**VARCHAR(n)**|Text up to `n` characters
**PRIMARY KEY**|Unique identifier per row — no duplicates
:::

sections.title: SELECT — Read Data
sections.body:
`SELECT` reads data — the command you will use most.

:::reminders
**SELECT * FROM users;**|All columns, all rows
**SELECT name, email FROM users;**|Only the columns you need
**SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 23;**|Filter rows
**SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY age ASC LIMIT 2;**|Sort + cap results
:::

Examples:
```sql
SELECT * FROM users;
SELECT name, email FROM users;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 23;
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY age ASC;
SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 2;
```

:::callout tip
Prefer naming columns over `*` in production — smaller result sets and clearer intent.
:::

sections.title: INSERT — Add New Data
sections.body:
`INSERT` adds new rows.

Single row:
```sql
INSERT INTO users (id, name, email, age)
VALUES (4, 'Ping', 'ping@example.com', 26);
```

Multiple rows:
```sql
INSERT INTO users (id, name, email, age)
VALUES
  (5, 'Noy', 'noy@example.com', 30),
  (6, 'Bee', 'bee@example.com', 25);
```

:::callout tip
Column order in the list must match value order in `VALUES` — mismatch causes wrong data or errors.
:::

sections.title: UPDATE — Change Existing Data
sections.body:
`UPDATE` changes existing rows — always scope with `WHERE`.

Safe update (one user):
```sql
UPDATE users
SET age = 25
WHERE id = 1;
```

Multiple columns:
```sql
UPDATE users
SET age = 25, email = 'newaoy@example.com'
WHERE id = 1;
```

:::compare
**With WHERE**|Only matching rows change — what you usually want.
**Without WHERE**|Every row in the table updates — a common production accident.
:::

Dangerous example:
```sql
UPDATE users SET age = 0;
```

:::callout warn
Run `SELECT * FROM users WHERE ...` first to verify which rows match before `UPDATE` or `DELETE`.
:::

sections.title: DELETE — Remove Data
sections.body:
`DELETE` removes rows — `WHERE` is required for safety.

Targeted deletes:
```sql
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 3;
DELETE FROM users WHERE age < 23;
```

:::compare
**DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 3;**|Removes matching rows only.
**DELETE FROM users;**|Removes every row — rarely what you want.
:::

Empty a whole table faster (structure stays):
```sql
TRUNCATE TABLE users;
```

:::callout warn
`DELETE` without `WHERE` wipes the table. In production, use transactions and backups before bulk deletes.
:::

sections.title: WHERE Conditions — Filter Like a Pro
What's Next?
sections.body:
You now have the **CRUD** core — Create, Read, Update, Delete:

:::reminders
**SELECT**|Read data
**INSERT**|Create rows
**UPDATE**|Change rows
**DELETE**|Remove rows
:::

:::steps
1) Practice on https://sqliteonline.com with a `users` table.
2) Learn **JOIN** to combine tables (orders + customers).
3) Add **indexes** when queries slow down on large data.
4) Model relationships with **foreign keys**.
:::

In fintech I use SQL daily — transaction history, account filters, report queries. Once it clicks, backend work gets much faster.
